families.s: HSE patient-hoist, sling compatibility and care-plan guidance
families.t: hoist selection, sling type and size, compatibility, loops, maintenance, surfaces, staffing, supervision and individual planning
f: Safe hoisting requires the correct hoist and sling for the person and task.
An undersized sling can cause discomfort and an oversized sling can allow a person to slip through.
Hoist and sling incompatibility can create insecure attachments.
Loop and leg configurations should follow manufacturer and care-plan instructions.
Hoists and slings require maintenance, inspection and applicable thorough examination.
A vulnerable person should not be left unattended in a hoist or an unsafe suspended position.
Difficult surfaces, long-distance travel or incorrect use can overturn a mobile hoist.
The individual assessment should specify equipment, sling, attachments, safety devices and the number of carers.
families.g: Hoisting risk depends on person and task, hoist and sling compatibility, size and attachment, floor and travel, carers, maintenance, examination, communication and supervision.

families.s: HSE healthcare and workplace sharps-injury prevention guidance
families.t: bloodborne viruses, safer devices, handling, no recapping, immediate disposal, containers, training, incident response and exposure follow-up
f: Blood-contaminated needles, blades and other sharps can transmit hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.
The assessment should identify how sharps are used, handled, passed, cleaned and disposed of.
A safer sharp device should be considered where the activity permits it.
Needles should not be bent, forced, resheathed or recapped unless a specific assessed method is essential.
Used sharps should be disposed of immediately into an appropriate sharps container.
Handling methods should keep points away from hands and use tools such as forceps where appropriate.
Workers need training in prevention, disposal and immediate response to an injury.
Post-exposure arrangements should provide prompt first aid, reporting, assessment and follow-up.
families.g: Sharps risk depends on device, contamination, procedure, hand position, patient movement, disposal point, safer technology, training, workload and post-exposure response.

families.s: HSE deliberate laboratory work with biological-agent containment guidance
families.t: hazard groups, deliberate use, COSHH assessment, containment, access, aerosols, incidents, notification, licensing and competent staff
f: Deliberate work includes intentional handling, propagation, processing or manipulation of biological agents.
This work commonly occurs in clinical, diagnostic, research and teaching laboratories.
Biological agents should be classified and assessed for hazards to human health.
Containment measures should match the agent, hazard group, procedure and aerosol or exposure potential.
Access, microbiological practice, equipment, ventilation, waste and decontamination should be controlled.
Incidents or accidents involving biological agents require planned response and investigation.
Certain deliberate work requires notification or licensing.
Workers require competence, information, training and health protection appropriate to the organisms and tasks.
families.g: Laboratory biological risk depends on agent and hazard group, concentration, procedure and aerosol generation, containment, equipment, access, decontamination, competence and incident response.

families.s: HSE Diving at Work Regulations and sector-ACOP guidance
families.t: project classification, diving contractor, team, supervisor, plan, medical fitness, breathing gas, decompression, chamber and records
f: The Diving at Work Regulations apply when one or more divers are at work, whether employed or self-employed.
Different approved codes apply to offshore, inland or inshore, media, scientific and recreational diving projects.
The correct project category determines the applicable team, equipment and procedural requirements.
A diving contractor and competent supervisor should plan, manage and control the project.
Divers need appropriate qualifications, competence and medical fitness.
The plan should cover breathing gas, communications, decompression, rescue and foreseeable emergencies.
Compression-chamber availability and time to treatment may be required according to the project and risk.
A diving operation record must contain the required particulars and be retained as required.
families.g: Diving risk depends on project type, depth and environment, breathing system, team and supervision, diver fitness, decompression, communications, rescue, chamber availability and records.

families.s: HSE adventure-activity licensing and provider-inspection guidance
families.t: licensable providers, under-18 participants, caving, climbing, trekking and watersports, safety management, application, inspection, licence conditions and public verification
f: The licensing scheme aims to assure good safety management for young people undertaking specified adventure activities.
Providers who sell in-scope activities to people under 18 must hold the required licence.
Licensable groups include specified caving, climbing, trekking and watersport activities.
A provider must determine whether each undertaking and centre falls within the scheme.
A licence must be held before the provider begins covered activities.
Applications should be submitted with enough time for documentation review and inspection.
Inspection examines safety policies, procedures, documents and site arrangements.
HSE can issue, vary, revoke or refuse licences to secure safety and publishes licence-holder information.
families.g: Adventure-activity risk depends on activity, location and weather, participant age and ability, instructors, equipment, supervision, emergency plans, provider systems and licence scope.
